parole.testo: From Proto-Germanic *fetjōjaną (“to surround, fit”) (whence also Dutch vitten (“to be suitable”), Old High German fizzōn (“to surround”)), from *fetjō (“foot, section”) + *-janą (“verbal suffix”) (the former whence Old Norse fit (“webbed foot of waterbirds”), Old English fitt (“song, poem”), Old Sax
From Proto-Germanic *galtjan (“to bay, bark”), from *gelt, dental extension of Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout”). See also Proto-Germanic *galaną (“to yell, shout”).
From Proto-Germanic *hluzô, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlus-ó-, from *ḱlew- (“to hear”).
From Proto-Germanic *hrahilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“to weave, beat”), cognate with English reel, Proto-Germanic *hragilą.

Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ludraz (“useless; worthless; bad”), according to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leut-, from *(s)lew- (“slack, loose, limp, flabby”). Compare Old English loddere, Old High German lotar (“vain; void; insignificant”), Middle High German lotter. See also
Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *raipą, *raipaz, from Proto-Indo-European *roypnós (“strap, band, rope”).
From Proto-Germanic *rōbǭ, *rōbijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rāp-yéh₂, from *(s)rā́ps (“turnip”). Cognate with German Rübe.

Related to the verb tölta (“to march in step”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *taltaz (“unsteady”), from Proto-Indo-European *del-, *dul- (“to shake, hesitate”), see also Dutch touteren (“to tremble”), North Frisian talt, tolt (“unstable, shaky”), Old English tealt (“unsteady”), tealtrian (“to shak
Inherited from Proto-Germanic *wīraz (“wire”) from Proto-Indo-European *weyro- (“a twist, thread, cord, wire”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y- (“to turn, twist, weave, plait”).
From ígull + ker. The first element is from Proto-Germanic *igilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰis (“hedgehog”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Probably; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: a thick winter coat (often with a fur-lined cap); a parka; an anorak
parole.testo: From archaic ólpa (“wide coat with cap”), of uncertain origin, though probably from a Proto-Germanic *wulpǭ (“woven garment”), from a Proto-Indo-European *welp- (“to bend, wrap around”), which appears to be a p-extension of *welH- (“to roll”), thus denoting a "rolled-up garment". See also Middle Eng
